newsitem.title: INDIA: Merrill hails India reforms, says outlook positive.
newsitem.headline: Merrill hails India reforms, says outlook positive.

text.p: Global investment bank Merrill Lynch on Thursday hailed India's economic reforms as one of the most successful among emerging markets and said the country's outlook was positive under the new government.
"India's macro-economic fundamentals are currently very positive," Merrill Lynch said in a global economics and currencies report on Thursday.

It said inflation was trending down, balance of payment position was sound, the rupee was stable, interest rates were expected to ease and the economy was becoming more open and better integrated with the global market.
A stable political environment and the committment of the new United Front coalition government, in power since June, to reforms was another positive factor.

Merrill said India faced a macro-economic crisis in 1991 and was on the verge of defaulting on its external debt obligations. The immediate trigger was a crisis in the balance of payments following a sharp plunge in foreign exchange reserves.
Credit agencies had downgraded India's credit rating and foreign capital inflows into India was suspended, it said.

"While the crisis was triggered in the external sector, there were serious macro-economic imbalances -- large fiscal and current account deficits, mounting public and external debt and double digit inflation," the report said.
It said the former P.V. Narasimha Rao government seized the opportunity presented by the crisis to introduce a series of structural reforms that radically altered India's course.

The reforms were wide ranging, encompassing fiscal policy, international trade and exchange rate policies, industrial policy and public enterprises, agricultural price and distribution policies, financial sector and capital markets.

"The speed and strength of India's recovery after the balance of payments crisis ranks among the most impressive recoveries by any emerging market that embarked on a reform programme following a macro-economic crisis," Merrill said.

Real GDP growth in India in the three years after the stabilisation programme was initiated in 1991/92 averaged 5.5 percent, compared to 5.1 percent in Thailand, 4.1 percent in Turkey, 2.14 percent in Kenya, 2.1 percent in Nigeria, 0.6 percent in Mexico and 2.2 percent for an average of 30 emerging markets, the Merrill report said.

In 1995/96, the economy grew at a robust 7.0 percent rate. Overall growth was led by a 11.7 percent growth rate in the industrial sector and a 7.0 percent growth in the services sector. Growth was strong despite a sluggish 2.4 percent increase in the agriculture sector, Merrill said.
It said trade reforms made India a more open economy. The export/GDP ratio doubled to 10 percent in 1995/96 (April-March) from 4.6 percent in 1985/86.
Investment reforms introduced in 1991 opened the way for increased foreign investment in India. Foreign capital flows surged to $4.1 billion in 1995/96 from $102 million in 1990/91.
Foreign investment as a share of GDP rose to 1.6 percent in 1994/95 from 0.6 percent in 1990/91.
"India is thus getting better integrated into global capital markets," the Merrill report said.
